questions.q: There is a blue bed in the room.
a: [יש מיטה כחולה בחדר|בחדר יש מיטה כחולה]
questions.why: The adjective follows its noun and copies its gender: מִיטָּה is feminine, so כְּחוּלָּה. The word יֵשׁ stays the same for anything at all, one bed or ten.

questions.q: My room is small and full of light.
questions.why: Possession is שֶׁל with an ending, after a noun with the article: הַחֶדֶר שֶׁלִּי, mine, against הַחֶדֶר שֶׁלּוֹ, his. The וְ turns into וּ before מ: וּמָלֵא.

questions.q: The lamp is old and yellow.
questions.why: Adjectives without the article after a definite noun make a sentence: הַמְּנוֹרָה יְשָׁנָה, 'the lamp is old'. With the article they only describe it: הַמְּנוֹרָה הַיְשָׁנָה, 'the old lamp'.

questions.q: The chair is behind the door.
questions.why: A thing already known needs no יֵשׁ: הַכִּיסֵּא מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַדֶּלֶת is complete without 'is'. A new, indefinite thing gets יֵשׁ, usually with the place first: מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַדֶּלֶת יֵשׁ כִּיסֵּא.

questions.q: Teo's mother is looking for the cat.
a: אִמָּא שֶׁל תֵּאוֹ מְחַפֶּשֶׂת אֶת הֶחָתוּל.
questions.why: The verb מְחַפֵּשׂ is pi'el, and its feminine ends in ־ֶת with a change of vowel before it: מְחַפֶּשֶׂת. The cat is definite, so it takes אֶת, and before ח the article is הֶ.

questions.q: Is there a computer in your room?
questions.why: A yes-no question is the statement said with a rising voice, so יֵשׁ מַחְשֵׁב? is already a question. To a boy it is שֶׁלְּךָ and to a girl שֶׁלָּךְ, spelled alike once the points are off.
The word אֵיפֹה opens the question and nothing stands in for 'are'. Teo is a boy, so 'your' is שֶׁלְּךָ; to his sister it would be שֶׁלָּךְ.

questions.q: The computer is on the table, next to the lamp.
questions.why: Both עַל and לְיַד take their noun straight after them, unlike מִתַּחַת, which needs לְ. Two place phrases can simply follow one another.

questions.q: There is nothing under the bed.
questions.why: Nothing is אֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר or אֵין כְּלוּם: the negative word sits inside an אֵין. The preposition מִתַּחַת takes לְ, which merges with the article: לַמִּיטָּה.

questions.q: The family's cat sleeps on Teo's bed.
a: הֶחָתוּל שֶׁל הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה יָשֵׁן עַל הַמִּיטָּה שֶׁל תֵּאוֹ.
החתול של המשפחה ישן [על המיטה|במיטה] של תאו
חתול המשפחה ישן [על המיטה|במיטה] של תאו
questions.why: Each owner gets its own שֶׁל, after a noun with the article: הֶחָתוּל שֶׁל הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה, הַמִּיטָּה שֶׁל תֵּאוֹ. Without the points, יָשֵׁן 'sleeps' and the passage's יָשָׁן 'old' are spelled alike.

questions.q: Teo comes in and looks under the bed.
questions.why: These are the masculine forms of the passage's נִכְנֶסֶת and מִסְתַּכֶּלֶת: נִכְנָס and מִסְתַּכֵּל. The וְ becomes וּ before מ.

questions.q: The old plates are under the bed.
questions.why: With the article on the adjective as well, הַצַּלָּחוֹת הַיְשָׁנוֹת is one phrase, 'the old plates', and the place completes the sentence. The adjective copies the noun's feminine plural ־וֹת.

questions.q: He has a computer, but he doesn't have a wardrobe.
a: יֵשׁ לוֹ מַחְשֵׁב, אֲבָל אֵין לוֹ אָרוֹן.
יש לו מחשב אבל אין לו ארון
יש לו מחשב אבל ארון אין לו
questions.why: Hebrew has no verb 'to have': it says יֵשׁ לְ, 'there is to', and אֵין לְ for the negative. The owner is an ending on the לְ: לוֹ him, לָהּ her, לִי me.

questions.q: There are two plates and an old book on the floor.
a: עַל הָרִצְפָּה יֵשׁ שְׁתֵּי צַלָּחוֹת וְסֵפֶר יָשָׁן.
על הרצפה יש [שתי|2] צלחות וספר ישן
יש [שתי|2] צלחות וספר ישן על הרצפה
questions.why: The noun צַלַּחַת is feminine, so two is שְׁתֵּי, the short form used before a noun. Each adjective agrees with its own noun only: סֵפֶר יָשָׁן is masculine.

questions.q: Teo doesn't see anything under the bed.
a: תֵּאוֹ לֹא רוֹאֶה כְּלוּם מִתַּחַת לַמִּיטָּה.
תאו לא רואה [כלום|שום דבר] מתחת למיטה
מתחת למיטה תאו לא רואה [כלום|שום דבר]
questions.why: After לֹא, the word כְּלוּם means 'anything': Hebrew negates twice where English negates once. The verb רוֹאֶה is the masculine present of לִרְאוֹת.
